svg.aria-label: Diagram: inbound and outbound DNS server policies in Google Cloud; an inbound policy creates entry points, internal IPv4 addresses taken from the primary range of every subnet in the network, so a network with two subnets in one region and a third in another gets three entry points, advertised by Cloud Router under default advertisement mode, and these addresses are not reachable across VPC Network Peering or Network Connectivity Center boundaries so a local policy is required in the network that terminates the hybrid connection, with the associated region for a query always the region of the tunnel or VLAN attachment that received the packets rather than the region of the subnet holding the entry point; an outbound policy replaces the resolution order rather than extending it, sending all queries to alternative name servers except those matched by a GKE cluster-scoped response policy or private zone, which means private zones, forwarding zones, peering zones and Compute Engine internal names all stop resolving; the plumbing requires TCP and UDP port 53 from 35.199.192.0/19, a reply from the configured server itself, and a return route whose next hop is in the same VPC network and the same region, though no symmetric path is required; and both directions can be configured at once on the same network
svg.title: DNS server policies: inbound adds addresses to ask, outbound replaces what answers
svg.text: Inbound adds addresses to ask. Outbound replaces everything that would have answered.
Same resource, same command, opposite blast radius.
INBOUND — entry points, one per subnet, that you did not choose
Entry points are internal IPv4 addresses “sourced from the PRIMARY IPv4 ADDRESS RANGE of EVERY
SUBNET” in the network. Two subnets in one region + a third elsewhere = 3 entry points.
You get no say in the addresses, and they move with your subnet layout. Proxy-only subnets and
Private NAT subnets are excluded.
Because they come from subnet ranges, Cloud Router advertises them under DEFAULT advertisement
mode. On CUSTOM mode you must include them yourself — #83 and #84, still binding.
No legacy networks. No IPv6-only subnets. Outbound on IPv6-only is fine.
An inbound policy ADDS a way to ask. It changes nothing about what the answers are.
Inbound: the two boundaries that are not routing problems
1. “Inbound DNS forwarding IP addresses are NOT REACHABLE across VPC Network Peering or Network
Connectivity Center (NCC) boundaries and require a LOCAL POLICY.” Put the policy in the
network that TERMINATES the tunnel. Reach records elsewhere with a DNS PEERING zone.
2. The associated REGION is the region of the TUNNEL that received the packets — “NOT the region
of the subnet containing the inbound server policy entry point.”
Tunnel in us-east1, entry point in us-west1: the query’s region is us-east1 — which is what a
geolocation routing policy will act on.
OUTBOUND — not an addition to the resolution order. A REPLACEMENT.
“Cloud DNS sends ALL QUERIES to the alternative name servers” — with one exception: a GKE
cluster-scoped response policy or cluster-scoped private zone.
“VMs in your VPC network are NO LONGER ABLE TO RESOLVE records in Cloud DNS private zones,
forwarding zones, peering zones, or Compute Engine internal DNS zones.”
Posts #98 and #99 built four mechanisms. One outbound policy switches all four off at once —
and “can also affect the resolution of PUBLIC DNS queries”, depending on what you point at.
The alternative name servers must now answer for EVERYTHING. Including your own VM names.
Outbound: the same four conditions as #99, plus a region
1. FIREWALL — “both TCP and UDP protocols with destination port 53 and 35.199.192.0/19 sources.”
2. ROUTES — static or dynamic, “except for static routes that only apply to VMs by network tag”.
And no policy-based route whose destination includes the name server address.
3. RETURN ROUTE — next hop in the SAME VPC NETWORK and the SAME REGION the query came from.
A different region in the same network is explicitly listed as a FAILING next hop.
Given that, “Google Cloud doesn’t require a symmetric return path” — any tunnel will do.
4. THE SERVER ITSELF must reply. A response from another name server is ignored.
A Type 1 server may NOT sit in a VPC network merely connected to yours. Same rule as #99.
Both at once is supported, and is the usual hybrid shape
“You can simultaneously configure inbound and outbound DNS forwarding for a VPC network.”
But prefer a FORWARDING ZONE over an outbound policy unless you really mean “all names”.
The one-line rule: a FORWARDING ZONE claims a suffix. An OUTBOUND SERVER POLICY claims the whole
namespace. Choosing the second when you meant the first is how a working estate loses every
internal name it had, in one apply, with no error.
